newsitem.title: UK: British right-wingers demand tough line on Europe.
newsitem.headline: British right-wingers demand tough line on Europe.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservatives, vowing they will win a fifth successive election, on Tuesday fought to claw back the opposition Labour party's huge poll lead with a pledge to crack down on young criminals.

But the party's bitter divisions over Europe came straight to the surface at its last pre-election conference, with so-called "Eurosceptics" calling on Prime Minister John Major to rule out British entry into a single European currency.

With just seven months before the deadline for an election, the conference amounts to Major's make-or-break bid to convince voters that the deeply unpopular Conservatives have not run out of steam after 17 years in power.
"This is a party that is on its way to winning the next election," party chairman Brian Mawhinney told anxious party members. "We must win and we will win."
Home Secretary (interior minister) Michael Howard tried to whip up enthusiasm among delegates with the standard Conservative conference fare of improving law and order.
He unveiled plans for a register of paedophiles and other sex offenders and a crackdown on clubs where drugs are sold. Police would be given powers to take alcohol from young people on the streets.
Howard promised to make stalking -- the obsessive following of women -- a criminal offence punishable by up to five years in jail.
"You don't become the party of law and order by calling yourself the party of law and order," he said, mocking Labour.
"You need to stand up for law and order, to take tough action to preserve it and to persevere with that action no matter how rough the going gets."
But right-wingers threatened to take spotlight away from the platform by demanding a tougher government line on Europe in meetings and speeches on the fringes of the conference.

Former treasury minister David Heathcoat-Amory, who quit his post earlier this year to campaign against monetary union, led the attack by telling a meeting: "Let us rule out now British participation in a single European currency.

"The proposal to give up the pound is a constitutional outrage and would be an economic disaster... We are sleepwalking towards a general election unable to make up our minds about an issue that will have to be decided next year."
Eurosceptics opposed to further integration with the EU have plagued Major's attempts to hold the party together in the face of a concerted attack from a revitalised Labour party.
Major has adopted a wait-and-see policy towards the single currency, saying he will decide after the next election if it is in Britain's interest to join
He is under pressure to rule out participation ahead of the election, a decision many advisers think would be a vote-winner.

Leon Brittan, a former Conservative cabinet minister, hit back at the European doubters. "If those hostile to the European Union wish to pursue the debate with integrity, it is time for them to declare their hand," said Brittan, now European Commission vice-president.
"Do they wish the United Kingdom to continue as a member of the EU, or would they like Britain to withdraw altogether?
"If that is the case, the enormous costs of non-membership need to be set out so that a clear judgement can be made."
Major's hopes of cutting Labour's lead have never looked worse after new allegations of corruption involving a former minister and last week's triumphal Labour conference.
An ICM opinion poll in the Guardian newspaper on Tuesday showed Labour had widened its lead to 18 points from 15.

A guerrilla attack on Monday on Britain's main army base in Northern Ireland also underscored the fragility of what many see as John Major's biggest achievement in six years as prime minister -- progress toward peace in the troubled province.
